family_judgments.evidence: The transformation item supplies “had locked” and therefore does not measure construction as the other formats do; the cloze/dialogue also have blocking response-key defects.
In the transformation format, past-perfect formation is converted into copying an explicitly supplied form, effectively redefining the construct as sentence assembly.
All formats retain Maya locking the office before the guard’s arrival.

criteria.evidence: The response requires the past perfect sequence had locked, activating past finite selection and participial perfect construction.
The simple-past arrival clause is appropriate supporting material for the declared past temporal relation.
The cue gives only the lemma lock, so the learner must select had and locked.
The prior mention of the office licenses either “had locked the office” or “had locked it.”
Solver-proposed “had locked it” is linguistically and contextually reasonable, but is unaccepted.
The item unnecessarily requires reproducing the object rather than merely supplying the target verb phrase, creating referential-form burden.
The required reply contains had + locked and therefore measures both declared operations.
The dialogue’s question and reply do not demand a separate grammatical construction from the learner.
The response slot does not provide the past-perfect form.
After “Maya secured it first,” “Maya had locked it before the guard arrived” is a natural completion.
“Had locked it” is a reasonable unkeyed response, yet only the repeated noun phrase is accepted.
The dialogue switches from secured to required lock and requires a specific object realization, adding lexical and reference burden.
A is distinguished by both had rather than has and locked rather than lock; the event-order context supports past perfect.
The comparison uses a transparent two-event past context without extra grammatical requirements.
Recognition and elimination of the visibly malformed options reduce construction evidence, but the keyed choice still represents both declared KCs.
A uniquely and clearly expresses the required earlier completed past action.
The single-choice key is complete; no solver proposed another acceptable option.
Office and guard vocabulary are common and the temporal relation is explicit.
The transformation cue explicitly supplies the complete target grammar chunk “had locked,” so success can be simple placement rather than selection of either declared form.
Combining two simple past statements with before does not introduce a major undeclared grammatical dependency.
The required past-perfect auxiliary and participle are both given verbatim in “use ‘had locked’,” allowing the learner to avoid constructing them.
The required beginning, supplied chunk, before, people, object, and event order constrain the intended sentence sufficiently.
No solver-proposed unkeyed alternative requires inclusion under the tightly constrained transformation cue.
The two source statements are short and semantically transparent.

summary: Cloze and dialogue reject the reasonable pronoun completion, and the transformation cue gives away the entire past-perfect target form.
